### Bridge Rectifier Working
A bridge rectifier uses four diodes ($D_1, D_2, D_3, D_4$) connected in a bridge configuration to provide full-wave rectification without needing a center-tapped transformer.
* **During Positive Half Cycle:** Diodes $D_1$ and $D_3$ are forward-biased and conduct current through load $R_L$, while $D_2$ and $D_4$ are reverse-biased.
* **During Negative Half Cycle:** Diodes $D_2$ and $D_4$ are forward-biased and conduct current through load $R_L$ in the same direction, while $D_1$ and $D_3$ are reverse-biased.

```text
Input:   ~ (Sinusoidal)
Output:  UU (Pulsating DC)
```

### Bridge Rectifier vs. Center-Tapped Rectifier
| Feature | Bridge Rectifier | Center-Tapped Rectifier |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Transformer Requirement** | Simple transformer (no center tap needed) | Requires a specialized center-tapped transformer |
| **Peak Inverse Voltage (PIV)** | $V_m$ | $2V_m$ |
| **Cost & Complexity** | Lower transformer cost, requires 4 diodes | Higher transformer cost, requires 2 diodes |
proTip: Bridge rectifiers have double the PIV rating advantage of center-tapped circuits, making them more economical for high-voltage applications.
